items.title: Kestra: The Next-Generation Workflow Orchestration Tool
items.author: Fauzan Ghaza
items.description:
Introduction

Workflow orchestration is a crucial aspect of modern data engineering and automation. With the rise of cloud-native applications and event-driven architectures, the need for a flexible, scalable, and easy-to-use orchestration tool has never been greater. Enter Kestra, a powerful open-source orchestration tool designed to simplify workflow automation for data engineers, DevOps teams, and software developers.

In this article, we will explore what Kestra is, its key features, how it compares to other workflow orchestration tools, and a simple guide to getting started.

What is Kestra?

Kestra is an open-source, declarative, event-driven workflow orchestration tool. It enables users to design, schedule, and monitor workflows through a YAML-based configuration system. Kestra is designed for cloud-native environments and supports various integrations, making it an excellent choice for data engineering, machine learning pipelines, and business process automation.

Key Features of Kestra

1. Declarative and Code-Driven Workflows

Kestra allows users to define workflows using YAML, making it simple and readable. The declarative approach ensures version control and easy collaboration.

2. Event-Driven Architecture

Unlike traditional batch scheduling tools, Kestra supports event-driven workflows, allowing tasks to be triggered by various events, such as API calls, database changes, or file uploads.

3. Scalability and Cloud-Native Support

Kestra is built with Kubernetes and cloud environments in mind. It can scale horizontally and integrate seamlessly with cloud services like AWS, GCP, and Azure.

4. Rich Integrations

Kestra provides built-in integrations with popular tools such as Apache Kafka, Airflow, dbt, PostgreSQL, and more, making it a versatile choice for modern data workflows.

5. User-Friendly Web Interface

Kestra offers an intuitive web UI for managing and monitoring workflows. Users can visualize workflow executions, logs, and dependencies in real-time.

6. Retries, Error Handling, and Observability

Kestra provides built-in mechanisms for task retries, failure notifications, and logging, ensuring high reliability for mission-critical workflows.

Kestra vs. Other Orchestration Tools

Kestra vs. Apache Airflow

  • Ease of Use: Kestra’s YAML-based configuration is simpler compared to Airflow’s Python-based DAGs.
  • Event-Driven: Kestra supports event-driven workflows, whereas Airflow primarily follows a batch-based model.
  • Scalability: Kestra is more lightweight and Kubernetes-native, making it easier to scale compared to Airflow’s CeleryExecutor-based approach.

Kestra vs. Prefect

  • Deployment: Kestra is Kubernetes-first, while Prefect can run locally and in the cloud.
  • Workflow Design: Kestra follows a declarative approach, whereas Prefect uses a Python-based imperative style.

Getting Started with Kestra

Prerequisites

Before starting, ensure you have Docker installed in your environment. We recommend using Docker for an easy setup.

Start Kestra with Docker

Run the following command to start Kestra in a Docker container:

docker run --pull=always --rm -it -p 8080:8080 --user=root \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  -v /tmp:/tmp kestra/kestra:latest server local

This command starts Kestra with an embedded H2 database, which does not persist data. If you need a persistent database like PostgreSQL, consider using Docker Compose for better configurability.

Access the Kestra UI

Once Kestra is running, open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. This is where you can build, manage, and monitor workflows.

Creating Your First Flow

Step 1: Navigate to Flows

On the left menu of the UI, go to Flows, then click Create.

Step 2: Define a Simple Workflow

Paste the following YAML configuration into the editor:

id: getting_started
namespace: company.team
tasks:
  - id: hello_world
    type: io.kestra.plugin.core.log.Log
    message: Hello World!

This simple workflow uses the Kestra Log plugin to print “Hello World!” in the logs.

Step 3: Execute the Workflow

Click Save, then hit Execute to run your first Kestra flow.

What’s Next?

Congratulations! 🎉 You’ve successfully installed Kestra and executed your first workflow. Now, explore more:

  • Follow the official tutorial.
  • Learn the core components of Kestra workflows.
  • Browse plugins to integrate with external systems.
  • Deploy Kestra in remote and production environments.
  • Customize configurations with the Administrator Guide

Conclusion

Kestra is a powerful and flexible workflow orchestration tool that simplifies automation for data engineers and developers. Its declarative approach, event-driven architecture, and seamless cloud integration make it an excellent choice for modern data workflows.

If you are looking for an alternative to Apache Airflow or Prefect that is easier to deploy and scale, give Kestra a try!

🔗 Learn More: https://kestra.io

items.title: Efficient Data Ingestion: Using Python to Stream Large Datasets into PostgreSQL
items.author: Fauzan Ghaza
items.description:
Streamline Your Data Workflow with Python and PostgreSQL

Handling large datasets can be a challenging task, especially when importing data into a database without overwhelming your system’s memory. In this article, I’ll walk you through a Python script that efficiently handles data ingestion by reading files in chunks and inserting them into a PostgreSQL database.

Introduction

Data ingestion is a critical step in data analytics and machine learning workflows. Whether you’re working with CSVs, Parquet files, or other formats, getting your data into a database quickly and efficiently is essential. This tutorial demonstrates how to:

  • Read large datasets without overloading memory.
  • Handle both CSV and Parquet file formats.
  • Insert data into a PostgreSQL database in chunks.

Let’s dive into the solution!

What This Script Does

The Python script automates the ingestion process with the following features:

  1. File Format Support: Handles both CSV and Parquet files.
  2. Chunk-Based Processing: Reads data in chunks to avoid memory overload.
  3. PostgreSQL Integration: Leverages SQLAlchemy for database connections and insertions.
  4. Command-Line Arguments: Offers customization for database credentials, file path, chunk size, and more.

Code Walkthrough

Below is the complete script with explanations for each key section.

1. Parameter Parsing with argparse

Using the argparse library, the script accepts user input via command-line arguments:

import argparse

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Ingest data into PostgreSQL")

parser.add_argument("--user", help="Postgres username", default="root")
parser.add_argument("--host", help="Database host", default="localhost")
parser.add_argument("--port", help="Database port", default="5432")
parser.add_argument("--db", help="Database name", default="ny_taxi")
parser.add_argument("--table", help="Target table name")
parser.add_argument("--url", help="Path to the data file (CSV or Parquet)")
parser.add_argument("--chunk", help="Chunk size for processing", default=10000, type=int)

args = parser.parse_args()

This approach allows flexibility, enabling users to adapt the script to various datasets and database configurations.

2. Reading the Data File

The script identifies the file format (CSV or Parquet) and reads the data accordingly:

import pandas as pd

def read_data(url, chunksize):
    if url.endswith(".csv"):
        print("File type: CSV")
        return pd.read_csv(url, iterator=True, chunksize=chunksize)
    elif url.endswith(".parquet"):
        print("File type: Parquet")
        df = pd.read_parquet(url)
        return [df[i:i + chunksize] for i in range(0, df.shape[0], chunksize)]
    else:
        raise ValueError("Unsupported file type: " + url)

3. Inserting Data into PostgreSQL

Using SQLAlchemy, the script connects to PostgreSQL and inserts data in chunks:

from sqlalchemy import create_engine
def insert_data(chunks, table, engine):
    for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks, start=1):
        print(f"Inserting batch {i}...")
        chunk["tpep_pickup_datetime"] = pd.to_datetime(chunk["tpep_pickup_datetime"])
        chunk["tpep_dropoff_datetime"] = pd.to_datetime(chunk["tpep_dropoff_datetime"])
        chunk.to_sql(name=table, con=engine, if_exists="append", index=False)

How to Use the Script

Follow these steps to use the script:

1. Install Dependencies

Ensure you have the required libraries installed:

pip install pandas sqlalchemy psycopg2 pyarrow

2. Save the Script

Save the script as data_ingestion.py.

3. Run the Script

Run the script with appropriate arguments. For example:

python data_ingestion.py \
    --user root \
    --host localhost \
    --db ny_taxi \
    --table yellow_taxi_data \
    --url path/to/your/file.csv \
    --chunk 10000

When prompted, enter the password for your PostgreSQL user.

Pipeline Overview

Below is a visual representation of the pipeline for this ingestion process:

Example Scenarios

Here are some scenarios where this script shines:

1. Handling Large CSV Files

When working with CSV files larger than your system’s memory, the script processes and inserts data in manageable chunks.

2. Integrating Parquet Files

Parquet files, known for their efficiency, are fully supported. The script reads the entire file and splits it into chunks.

3. Preprocessing During Ingestion

You can modify the script to preprocess data (e.g., handling missing values or normalizing columns) during ingestion.

Challenges and Solutions

Challenge: Ingestion is slow for very large datasets.

Solution: Optimize PostgreSQL performance by:

  • Disabling indexes temporarily during insertion.
  • Using bulk inserts.

Challenge: Unsupported file formats.

Solution: Extend the script to handle formats like JSON or XML.

Conclusion

This script provides a robust and scalable solution for ingesting large datasets into PostgreSQL. By leveraging Python’s data processing capabilities and SQLAlchemy’s database integration, you can handle files of any size with ease.

Feel free to adapt this script to your specific workflows. If you have questions or suggestions, share them in the comments below — I’d love to hear your thoughts!

items.title: Virtual Machines vs. Containers
items.author: Fauzan Ghaza
items.description:
Understanding the Foundations of Modern Computing

The debate between Virtual Machines (VMs) and Containers has been a cornerstone of modern computing, shaping how applications are deployed and scaled. Whether you’re diving into DevOps, cloud computing, or software development, understanding the distinction between these technologies is essential.

In this article, I’ll break down the key differences, advantages, and disadvantages of both to help you grasp their use cases and make informed decisions.

What Are Virtual Machines?

Virtual Machines emulate an entire physical computer system, including its hardware, allowing multiple operating systems to run on the same hardware.

Key Characteristics:

  • Isolation:
    VMs are highly isolated, with each running its own OS. This ensures that an issue in one VM doesn’t impact others.
  • Flexibility:
    Run different operating systems (e.g., Linux, Windows) on the same hardware, making them ideal for legacy systems or multi-OS environments.
  • Resource Usage:
    VMs require substantial resources since each instance includes a full OS, leading to higher memory and storage overhead.

Use Cases:

  • Hosting multiple operating systems on a single server.
  • Running legacy applications that require specific OS environments.
  • Testing software in isolated, sandboxed environments.

What Are Containers?

Containers package an application and its dependencies into a lightweight, portable unit. Unlike VMs, containers share the host OS, making them more efficient.

Key Characteristics:

  • Lightweight:
    Containers run without the overhead of a full operating system, sharing the host OS kernel instead.
  • Fast Startup:
    Since they don’t need to boot an entire OS, containers start and stop almost instantly.
  • Portability:
    Containers can run anywhere, whether it’s your local machine, a cloud server, or a Kubernetes cluster.

Use Cases:

  • Deploying microservices in modern application architectures.
  • Scaling applications horizontally with minimal resource usage.
  • Building Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipelines.

Key Differences

Here’s a side-by-side comparison of Virtual Machines and Containers:

Visual Summary:

Which One Should You Use?

The choice between VMs and Containers depends on your specific needs:

  • Choose VMs if you require strong isolation, need to run different operating systems, or have legacy software dependencies.
  • Choose Containers if you want lightweight, portable, and scalable solutions for modern application deployment.

Final Thoughts

Virtual Machines and Containers each have their place in modern computing. Understanding their differences is crucial to designing efficient, scalable, and cost-effective systems.

Which one do you use most in your workflow, and why? Let me know in the comments below!

items.title: Building a Stress Prediction System with Machine Learning and MLOps
items.author: Fauzan Ghaza
items.description:
Introduction

Access to potable water is a critical global issue that affects millions of lives every day. The ability to predict water potability can help communities make informed decisions and ensure safer access to clean water. Recognizing this need, our team developed a robust machine learning (ML) service designed to analyze and predict water potability. This project emphasized scalability, security, and reproducibility by integrating cutting-edge tools and frameworks.

Water potability analysis is vital in identifying safe drinking water sources. Traditional methods often require manual sampling and testing, which can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. By leveraging machine learning, we aimed to provide a faster, more efficient way to analyze water potability using a scalable and automated system.

System Architecture

Our solution integrates several modern tools and frameworks to ensure a seamless and scalable implementation. Below is an overview of the system architecture:

  • 🔍 MLflow (Experiment Tracking and Artifact Management): MLflow was employed to track and manage machine learning experiments. It allowed us to maintain reproducibility, version control, and efficient artifact storage.
  • 📦 MinIO (Secure Cloud Storage): MinIO, a high-performance object storage solution, was used to store datasets and model artifacts. Its S3 compatibility ensured secure and reliable access to data.
  • 🗂 PostgreSQL with pgAdmin (Metadata Repository): PostgreSQL was utilized as a metadata repository to manage structured data, while pgAdmin provided an intuitive interface for database management.
  • 🐋 Docker Compose (Container Orchestration): All system components, including MLflow, MinIO, and PostgreSQL, were containerized using Docker Compose. This ensured simplified deployment and scalability.

Deployment

To enable seamless communication between components, we utilized gRPC, a high-performance, open-source remote procedure call (RPC) framework. The benefits included:

  • ⚡ Speed: gRPC ensured low-latency communication, critical for real-time ML predictions.
  • 📈 Scalability: Its efficient serialization (Protocol Buffers) allowed the service to handle large-scale deployments with ease.

Conclusion

This project taught us valuable lessons about integrating MLOps and cloud-native tools into real-world machine learning systems:

  1. MLOps Is Essential: Tools like MLflow and Docker Compose streamline the development and deployment lifecycle, ensuring reproducibility and scalability.
  2. Security Matters: Using MinIO and environment variables enhanced the system’s security and reliability.
  3. Collaboration Wins: Combining expertise across data science, DevOps, and software engineering led to an efficient and innovative solution.

Our water potability ML service exemplifies how integrating modern tools and frameworks can solve real-world problems efficiently. From experiment tracking to scalable deployment, the project demonstrates the power of MLOps in building impactful solutions.

Explore the full implementation and architecture details on GitHub.

Let’s create a safer, more sustainable future together — one drop at a time.

  • 📈 Scalability: Its efficient serialization (Protocol Buffers) allowed the service to handle large-scale deployments with ease.

Conclusion

This project taught us valuable lessons about integrating MLOps and cloud-native tools into real-world machine learning systems:

  1. MLOps Is Essential: Tools like MLflow and Docker Compose streamline the development and deployment lifecycle, ensuring reproducibility and scalability.
  2. Security Matters: Using MinIO and environment variables enhanced the system’s security and reliability.
  3. Collaboration Wins: Combining expertise across data science, DevOps, and software engineering led to an efficient and innovative solution.

Our water potability ML service exemplifies how integrating modern tools and frameworks can solve real-world problems efficiently. From experiment tracking to scalable deployment, the project demonstrates the power of MLOps in building impactful solutions.
